newsitem.title: USA: Lake hearing for CIA delayed to Clinton's dismay.
newsitem.headline: Lake hearing for CIA delayed to Clinton's dismay.

text.p: The head of the Senate Intelligence Committee on Tuesday postponed confirmation hearings for Anthony Lake, President Bill Clinton's nominee to head the Central Intelligence Agency, for the second time.

Chairman Richard Shelby, an Alabama Republican, said his panel would delay the session until March 11 while it looked into the "many unanswered, perplexing questions that remain" about Lake, Clinton's former national security adviser.
Clinton talked to Shelby by phone and urged him to reconsider, the White House said.

In a move branded as purely partisan by Lake supporters, Shelby initially postponed the confirmation hearings until the week of Feb. 25 while the Justice Department finished probes of Lake's stock dealings and disputed congressional testimony.
In a statement, Shelby criticised the Justice Department, which ended the two investigations on Friday. The probes had been hurdles to Lake's confirmation by the Republican-led Senate.
Clinton, during a visit to Capitol Hill, talked by phone to Shelby to reiterate his strong support for Lake.

"The president was concerned to learn during the call that Sen. Shelby intends to delay Mr. Lake's confirmation hearing and urged that Sen. Shelby consider holding the hearing sooner," the White House said.

"The president said he was confident that Tony and the White House could resolve any remaining questions on the issues that Sen. Shelby has identified," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said in a statement.

McCurry earlier expressed frustration at the new delay in Lake's confirmation hearings, saying Clinton has "an ample need to have strong leadership within the intelligence community as we move into the weeks ahead."
Lake would succeed John Deutch to become head of the CIA, the lead U.S. spy agency, and the director of central intelligence who oversees 12 other agencies.
He agreed on Friday to pay $5,000 to settle a civil inquiry into whether his failure to promptly sell energy stocks violated federal conflict-of-interest laws.

The Justice Department on the same day announced it had found "no basis for any criminal charges" against Lake arising from testimony he gave in September about the administration's policy of turning a blind eye to Iranian arms shipments to Bosnian Moslems in 1994.

"While the Justice Department's report issued last Friday will certainly be considered, it raises as many questions as it purported to answer, and was not as satisfactory as I had hoped," Shelby said.
An aide said he was referring to a combined report on the matters submitted by the Justice Department to the panel.

Shelby said the department had failed to address the purchase by Lake's broker of stock in the Williams Co., an energy-related firm. He asserted that the $5,000 Lake paid to settle the matter of his stock trading was "inconsistent" with his profits as well as with existing law.

Lake has acknowledged failing for two years to sell specified shares after being told by the White House counsel's office in 1993 to divest to avoid any possible conflict of interest in the performance of his duties. As national security adviser, he helped shape U.S.-Mideast policy with a potential impact on the value of energy firms.
